title: Charge moves; neutral objects respond
question: If both objects start neutral, can rubbing create net charge?
explanation: Electrons move between objects; count the equal positive deficit and negative excess. A nearby neutral object can polarise.
limits: Counted charges and displacements are enlarged. Polarisation force is a qualitative proxy, not a molecular simulation.

title: Inside a conducting shell
question: Does a metal shell merely weaken the external electric field?
explanation: Inspect external and induced fields separately, then add them: the empty cavity is field-free in electrostatic equilibrium.
limits: Analytic conducting sphere in a uniform static field. The cutaway is a view, not a physical opening; this does not model radio-frequency shielding.

title: Slow electrons, fast signal
question: Must an electron travel from the battery to the LED before the LED responds?
explanation: The wire already contains mobile charge. A signal travels through the circuit much faster than the average electron drift.
limits: Illustrative 1 m wire, signal speed 10^8 m/s and chosen drift speed 0.1 mm/s; the two clocks have separate labelled scales.

title: Find the dark LED
question: Can a battery show its normal voltage and still fail under load?
explanation: An exponential LED model and source load line meet at the measured operating point. Open and reverse states alter the visible circuit.
limits: Illustrative exponential I–V with nVt=0.08 V, calibrated to 20 mA at red 2.0 V / white 3.3 V; temperature, leakage, reverse breakdown and component specifications omitted.

title: Measure two branches
question: Do unequal parallel branches have equal current or equal voltage?
explanation: Change the actual series/parallel topology, then inspect branch/total current or the red–black voltage difference across either load.
limits: Ideal resistors and fixed 2 V LED drops in this topology lesson; these are separate from the nonlinear diagnostic model.

title: A fault in the case
question: Does a small current leaking to earth look like an overload?
explanation: Compare a protective-earth fault, isolated live case, virtual touch return and balanced overload. A trip opens the actual switch and stops current until reset.
limits: Prescribed prospective fault current, ideal latched 30 mA imbalance / 16 A overload comparisons, no real trip timing or body-resistance prediction; all routes are virtual.

title: Domains inside a magnet
question: When a magnet is cut, can one half contain only a north pole?
explanation: Domain orientations and their net moment change with the applied field. Cutting the sample leaves complete dipoles on both pieces.
limits: Schematic domains: field-dependent orientation and favourable-region growth, not a quantitative hysteresis or atomic-spin model.

title: A compass that can dip
question: Does a compass reveal the complete direction of Earth’s field?
explanation: A free needle aligns in three dimensions. A level compass can show only the horizontal projection; device axes rotate while the world field stays fixed.
limits: Centred ideal dipole, not a local geomagnetic forecast. Latitude controls the ideal dip, which differs from measured Mumbai values.

title: Add wire and Earth fields
question: Will reversing the wire current turn a compass exactly 180 degrees?
explanation: Move the probe and add the wire field to a fixed northward background. Compare the separate vectors and their sum.
limits: Long straight wire, 38.4 microtesla horizontal background. The tram preset treats one distant current and omits the return conductor. Coil contributions use the on-axis Biot–Savart field of circular loops of 1 cm radius, spaced 1 mm apart. The centre probe is fixed in that mode; field-arrow scales are printed separately.

title: Step inside a motor
question: Why must the current reverse every half-turn?
explanation: Opposite coil sides carry opposite currents and feel opposite forces. The split ring reverses current so torque keeps the same rotational sense.
limits: Uniform 0.5 T field, 10 turns of 0.04 m² area. Rotor inertia 0.08 kg·m² and damping 0.35 s^-1 are chosen model values; ideal instantaneous commutation. Holding freezes the rotor for inspection; open circuit removes electrical torque while a moving rotor coasts. Back emf is omitted.

title: Turn a generator
question: Does the largest flux always mean the largest induced voltage?
explanation: Rotating a coil changes flux. The voltage tracks the rate of flux change, reaching zero at maximum or minimum flux.
limits: Uniform field, ideal coil; mechanical rotation is supplied externally. Loading and self-inductance are omitted.

title: Two coils, one changing field
question: Can a steady direct current keep inducing voltage in a second coil?
explanation: Both coils link the same reversing flux. Blue primary and red secondary emf follow its time derivative; changing turns changes their amplitude ratio.
limits: AC control is RMS voltage, with an ideal resistive secondary load and no core losses/saturation. Separate steady DC comparison assumes 10 Ω primary winding resistance and schematic stored flux; switching transient omitted.

title: Two fields across a gap
question: Does either field point along the wave’s travel direction?
explanation: Inspect electric and magnetic field vectors at fixed points. Both are transverse, perpendicular to one another and in phase.
limits: Plane wave; amplitudes use independent diagram scales. Wavelength spans are normalised and the animation is enormously slowed.

title: Earth turns beneath the sky
question: Which way must Earth turn for stars to seem to move west?
explanation: A marked surface observer crosses the lit and dark hemispheres. Change from a space camera to a surface-direction diagram.
limits: Ideal sphere and distant Sun; solar time, not Mumbai civil time. Star coordinates are illustrative.

title: Tilt, sunlight and daylight
question: If tilt is zero but the orbit remains, do the seasons remain?
explanation: Keep the axis fixed in space as Earth moves round its orbit. Link latitude, local noon altitude, daylight arc and a beam footprint.
limits: Circular orbit isolates tilt; daily geometry is approximate and ignores refraction and weather.

title: The Moon has to turn
question: Would a Moon that never rotated always show us the same face?
explanation: Keep a marked face directed towards Earth by rotating it once per orbit. Compare with a non-rotating sphere and follow its illuminated half.
limits: Circular orbit with schematic sizes. Lunar libration is omitted; this is not a dated Moon-rise calculator.

title: Find an eclipse by geometry
question: Why can a new Moon miss the Sun–Earth line?
explanation: Advance orbital longitude and the year. The inclined lunar plane meets the ecliptic at two nodes; shadow intersections are calculated from these positions.
limits: Circular orbits and fixed nodes; no dated ephemeris. Earth, Moon, orbital distance and calculated shadow widths share one scale in 3D. The finite Sun is outside the display; the 2D view compresses the orbital gap and magnifies the height.

title: Subtract Earth’s central pull
question: Why is there an outward relative pull on the far side?
explanation: Inspect the Moon’s absolute pull and subtract the pull at Earth’s centre at each surface point. Add the Sun’s differential pull.
limits: Ideal equilibrium tide pattern, with arrows hugely enlarged. Continents, ocean dynamics and Haji Ali timing are not predicted.

title: Count photons and electrons
question: Can bright red light beat the threshold by pooling its photons?
explanation: Frequency sets energy per photon and maximum electron kinetic energy; photon flux sets the number available. Retarding voltage reveals the stopping potential.
limits: Single-photon calcium model with work function 2.71 eV. A uniform 0-to-maximum electron-energy distribution is illustrative; multiphoton effects are outside this model.

title: An atom is mostly space
question: If a nucleus were a 1 cm marble, how large would the atom be?
explanation: Change the scale and compare a nucleus reference width with the electron-cloud reference width. Electrons are not drawn on planetary tracks.
limits: Approximate 10^5 diameter ratio; a cloud outline is a probability-region symbol rather than a solid boundary.

title: Exposure, contamination and decay
question: Does switching off a beam remove radioactive dust?
explanation: Compare a controlled beam with radioactive material left on a surface. Individual random decay times produce a smooth exponential expectation only in a large ensemble.
limits: Simulated decay events; half-life is chosen in arbitrary model seconds. No dose or biological-effect calculation.

title: From the solar core to light
question: Does the Sun’s light come from chemical burning at its surface?
explanation: Open a solar cutaway, inspect the net fusion account and compare the released mass fraction with the total. Energy crosses radiative and convective layers.
limits: Net reaction and atomic masses are bookkeeping. Transport is a schematic stage sequence, not a simulated photon diffusion time.

title: A halo around L1
question: Is L1 a place where gravity is zero?
explanation: Inspect linked xy/xz/yz projections of the same craft point. Independently compare Sun/Earth force balance at the selected distance.
limits: Point masses for the force account; its distance control does not relocate the independently schematic 177.86-day halo. No mission ephemeris or integrated restricted-three-body orbit.

title: Same hydrogen, different lines
question: Does a weak hydrogen line mean little hydrogen?
explanation: Hold composition fixed and change temperature; hydrogen ionisation and excitation compete. Then change abundance separately.
limits: LTE Saha–Boltzmann population proxy at fixed electron density 10^20 m^-3, ground-state partition approximation. Line depths are illustrative, not an atmosphere fit.

title: From a blink to a distance
question: Can a star look faint because it is distant rather than weak?
explanation: Change the exaggerated-angle baseline/triangle and uncertainty, then follow one shared Cepheid time/phase through the star and flux curve.
limits: Triangle uses logarithmic distance and exaggerated angles; numerical parallax is physical. Cepheid relation and icon radius/colour are illustrative; extinction, metallicity and calibration uncertainty omitted.

title: More mass, smaller dwarf
question: Does adding material always make a star bigger?
explanation: Move along an ideal white-dwarf mass–radius relation. Compare core mass with initial stellar mass and stop at the stable-model limit.
limits: Zero-temperature ideal relation with 1.44-solar-mass limiting mass. Zero radius marks model breakdown, not a physical white dwarf of zero size.

title: Choose another galaxy
question: If every distant galaxy recedes, are we at the centre?
explanation: Select any galaxy and expand separations. Every observer finds the same distance–recession relation while individual bound-galaxy sizes stay fixed.
limits: Homogeneous low-redshift Hubble-flow model; local peculiar velocities and general-relativistic light propagation are omitted.

title: A pendulum and a turning Earth
question: Would a Foucault pendulum precess equally in Mumbai and at the equator?
explanation: Compare local floor traces as latitude changes. The precession rate is Earth’s rotation projected onto the local vertical.
limits: Small-amplitude ideal pendulum; precession is the local approximation, not a claim of one globally fixed swing plane at every latitude.

title: An axle parallel to Earth’s
question: Why does Ooty’s latitude match the telescope’s slope?
explanation: Tilt the telescope axle to the selected latitude, then compare it with Earth’s axis. Change mesh spacing relative to wavelength.
limits: Equatorial-mount geometry is exact; mesh reflection is a qualitative wavelength comparison, not an electromagnetic solver.

title: Read a track through emulsion
question: Can a flat microscope image hide motion through the plate?
explanation: Compare simulated resolved grains with the matching projection. Independently select observed RMS scattering and finite position resolution to infer a mass/speed interval at known momentum.
limits: Highland x/X₀=.01 proxy, 1/β² grain-density proxy; transverse magnification and resolution are labelled. Interval conditions on known momentum/material and omits energy loss and sampling uncertainty. This does not reconstruct historical plates.

title: Nature and its mirror
question: Does a mirror image of the weak-decay pattern remain an allowed pattern?
explanation: Reverse spin alignment and compare electron counts. In a mirror, spin is an axial vector while electron velocity is a polar vector; their correlation changes.
limits: Illustrative angular asymmetry parameter 0.8, not historical count data. Nuclear spin is an arrow, not a classical spinning ball.

title: Count states, not labels
question: Does exchanging two identical photons produce a new state?
explanation: Exchange actual red A/blue B positions, then remove labels for bosons and apply the same-spin fermion exclusion.
limits: Fixed two particles, two available one-particle states; no fixed-total-energy constraint. Counts alone do not assign general probabilities or derive Planck’s law.

title: Measure a tiny displaced star
question: Does one noisy measurement prove a theory?
explanation: Change angular resolution and compare apparent positions against zero, half-Einstein and Einstein deflection predictions, with uncertainty shown explicitly.
limits: Solar-limb general-relativistic deflection 1.75 arcseconds, scaled by inverse impact parameter. The plot is simulated evidence, not the 1919 plates. The 3D ray bend is enlarged for inspection; use the labelled arcsecond plot for measurement.
